passage:
Diary, Sunday night. Sarita.

First shift at the hospice today. It's been a year since Papa. Two years of his illness before that, and me at his bedside every evening after work.

Today I sat with a man named Mr Fernandes and read him the newspaper, and helped the nurse turn his pillow. He squeezed my hand when I left. On the bus home I felt something I haven't felt in a year: useful. Like all those evenings with Papa taught me something I can give.

Then I got home and saw Papa's grey shawl on the chair. And I cried for an hour. The volunteering didn't fix that part.

I think both things are true. This can be my purpose. But I still need to miss him, properly, separately.

Called Kishore bhaiya. We talked about Papa till midnight.

qa.q: Whose grey shawl was on the chair?
qa.a: Papa's.

qa.q: Why did Sarita cry after such a meaningful day?
qa.a: The volunteering gave purpose, but seeing Papa's shawl brought the grief back, showing Sarita that the sadness still needs its own space.

qa.q: What else could help Sarita alongside the hospice work?
qa.a: Keeping time just for missing Papa, like talking with Kishore bhaiya, and seeking a grief counsellor if it feels too heavy.

qa.q: How might Mr Fernandes feel about Sarita's visit?
qa.a: Mr Fernandes likely felt comforted and cared for, which is why he squeezed Sarita's hand.

grounding: Shows an adult who lost a parent to a long illness finding purpose in hospice volunteering while the grief still needs its own space.

passage: In the small town of Palakkad, the palliative care unit ran on volunteers, and Nirmala came every Tuesday and Friday. Her father had spent three years dying slowly of a lung illness, and she'd learnt to change sheets, to sit quietly, to hold a hand. Now she did it for others. It felt like her father's suffering had turned into something useful. One Friday, an old man in bed four reached for her hand, and his knuckles looked exactly like her father's. She finished her shift. Then she went and sat by the temple pond and cried until the lamps were lit. Kishore, a senior volunteer, found her there. He sat down. "The work doesn't replace the grieving," he said. "We have a circle on Sundays, for volunteers who've lost someone. You'd be welcome." Nirmala nodded, wiping her face. She went that Sunday.

qa.q: How long had Nirmala's father been ill?
qa.a: Three years.

qa.q: Why did the old man's knuckles make Nirmala cry?
qa.a: They looked exactly like her father's, bringing back grief that the caring work had given purpose to but not healed.

qa.q: Why was Kishore's suggestion helpful?
qa.a: The Sunday circle gives Nirmala a separate place to grieve, so the caring work doesn't have to hold all her sadness.

qa.q: How might the old man in bed four have experienced Nirmala's care?
qa.a: He probably felt comforted and less alone, reaching for her hand without knowing what it stirred in her.

grounding: Shows an adult who lost a parent to a long illness finding purpose in palliative care volunteering while learning the grief still needs its own space.

passage:
Dear diary, it's Sharmila.

Today in science Miss asked me to read the paragraph about plants. I got stuck on "photosynthesis." I said "photo-sin-thesis" and someone giggled. My face went HOT. So I made a fish face, puffed my cheeks and said, "Photo-fishy-thesis!" Everybody laughed, even Miss a little. Parul laughed so much she snorted.

It felt good. Like I was in charge of the laughing, not them.

But now it's bedtime and my tummy feels tight. Tomorrow is reading again. I don't want to make a fish face every day.

I think I'll ask Amma to practise the hard words with me tonight. Just a few.

qa.q: Which word did Sharmila get stuck on?
qa.a: "Photosynthesis."

qa.q: Why did Sharmila make a fish face after stumbling?
qa.a: Sharmila felt embarrassed when someone giggled, and turning it into a joke felt like taking control of the laughing.

qa.q: What small step is Sharmila planning, and why might it help?
qa.a: Practising the hard words with Amma, which tackles the reading worry underneath instead of relying on jokes.

qa.q: How might Parul have felt laughing at the fish face?
qa.a: Parul probably felt amused and happy, not realising Sharmila was covering embarrassment.

grounding: Shows a child who stumbles while reading making a silly face to get the class laughing along, though the clowning covers a worry.

passage: In the village school near Bathinda, the teacher asked Baljeet to read the Punjabi poem aloud. He got the first line wrong, then the second. He stopped. Then he clutched his heart, rolled his eyes and fell dramatically sideways off the bench. "The poem has defeated me!" The whole class roared. Nitin, beside him, laughed until he cried. Even the teacher smiled. But she'd noticed something. Baljeet always did a funny act when it was his turn to read: a sneeze, a voice, a faint. Never when it was maths or games. After class she called him over. "You're very funny. Is reading hard for you?" Baljeet's grin slipped for a second. "No, Ma'am." Then, quietly, "A bit." She nodded. "Stay for ten minutes on Thursdays. Just you and me."

qa.q: What did Baljeet do after getting the second line wrong?
qa.a: He clutched his heart, rolled his eyes and fell dramatically sideways off the bench.

qa.q: Why does Baljeet always do a funny act when it's his turn to read?
qa.a: Reading makes him feel anxious and embarrassed, and making the class laugh lets him stay in control instead of showing he's struggling.

qa.q: What did the teacher do that could help Baljeet most?
qa.a: She noticed the pattern, gently asked about reading privately, and offered extra time on Thursdays.

qa.q: How might Nitin see Baljeet's performances?
qa.a: Nitin probably sees them as hilarious and doesn't guess they hide worry about reading.

grounding: Shows a child who stumbles reading aloud clowning to get the class laughing with him, while the teacher notices the worry beneath.

passage: In the classroom in São Paulo, Paulo stood to read his history paragraph and tripped over "independence." He tried again. "Indepen... indep..." Someone at the back snorted. Paulo froze, then switched to a robot voice. "ERROR. WORD. TOO. LONG. REBOOTING." The class exploded with laughter. Alejandro nearly fell off his chair. Paulo sat down grinning and took a bow. At break, Alejandro was still laughing. "You're so funny, man. You always do that." Paulo kicked at the ground. "Yeah." "Wait, do you do it on purpose?" Paulo was quiet. "When I get stuck, everyone's looking. If I make them laugh, it's like I chose it." Alejandro stopped laughing. "Oh." Paulo shrugged. "Doesn't matter." But he didn't do the robot for the rest of the day.

qa.a: "Independence."

qa.q: Why did Paulo switch to a robot voice?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed with everyone looking, and making them laugh felt like he had chosen the moment instead of failing at it.

qa.q: How could Alejandro support Paulo now that he knows?
qa.a: Alejandro could avoid pushing him to be funny when reading, and maybe practise hard words with him or suggest he talk to the teacher.

qa.a: Alejandro stops laughing, seeing that the jokes cover worry, not just fun.

passage: Tejas, you asked why I've stopped joking about my braces. Okay, here's Charu's honest version. When I got them in class nine, I decided to get in first. Before anyone could say anything, I'd say, "Hi, I'm a walking fence," or, "Don't stand near me in a thunderstorm." Everyone laughed. It worked. People liked me. Nobody could hurt me with something I'd already said. But after a few months, it changed. People started saying the jokes to me. "Oi, metal mouth." "Fence girl." And they weren't laughing with me anymore. They'd learnt from me that my braces were fair game. That was the day I realised I'd taught them how to treat me. So now I just don't mention them. If someone does, I say, "Not funny," and change the subject.

qa.q: What joke did Charu make about the braces?
qa.a: "A walking fence."

qa.q: Why did Charu joke about the braces before anyone else could?
qa.a: Charu felt nervous and self-conscious, and joking first felt like protection, because nobody could hurt Charu with something already said.

qa.q: What did Charu change, and why is it a good step?
qa.a: Charu stopped the self-mocking jokes and started saying "Not funny," which stops others treating the braces as fair game.

qa.q: How might classmates have started to see Charu over those months?
qa.a: Some classmates came to see Charu as an easy target, because the jokes had shown them the braces were open to mockery.

grounding: Shows a teenager mocking their own braces before anyone else could, winning acceptance but teaching others to treat them as a target.

passage:
Monday: The maths results came out. Before anyone could ask, Ojas stood on his chair. "Thirty-two out of hundred! Someone call the newspapers!" The class laughed. Ojas bowed.
Wednesday: In chemistry, he did it again. "Fourteen out of fifty! A new record! Keep the trophies coming!" More laughter. His friend Usha didn't laugh.
Friday: In the corridor, two boys he barely knew shouted, "Oi, Zero Ojas! Got any new records?" and laughed at him, not with him. Ojas laughed along, but it came out thin. At lunch, Usha sat next to him. "You taught them that name, you know." Ojas stared at his tiffin. "I just didn't want them to say it first." "I know. But now they're saying it anyway." Ojas didn't make a joke for the rest of the day.

passage: Tejas, you keep making jokes about your weight at school. Your Jatin mama wants to tell you something. When I was fifteen, in Mysuru, I had very big ears. I decided that if I joked first, nobody could hurt me. So on the first day of class ten, I said, "Don't worry, I can hear you from the back row. Built-in speakers." The class loved it. passage:
Dear diary, Pranav here.

Today was the robotics demo. Our line-following robot, which took us eight weeks, went straight off the table in front of the judges and crashed into the dustbin. Then a wire caught and the whole thing started smoking.

Silence. Then Vinita said, "Well, at least it's recycled now." And we all cracked up. Properly. Tears. Even one judge laughed.

It still hurt. Eight weeks. But after laughing, we could actually look at it. We sat on the lab floor and made a list: the sensor was loose, the wire was too close to the motor, the code had a bug. The judges said we can re-demo on Friday.

If we hadn't laughed, I think we'd have just gone home and felt terrible separately.

qa.q: How long had the team worked on the robot?
qa.a: Eight weeks.

qa.q: Why did laughing help Pranav and the team?
qa.a: The laughter gave them some distance from the disappointment, so they could look at the problem without feeling crushed.

qa.q: What did the team do after laughing, and why does it matter?
qa.a: They sat on the lab floor and listed what went wrong, turning the moment into a plan for the Friday re-demo.

qa.q: How might the judge who laughed see the team?
qa.a: The judge probably saw them as resilient and good-humoured, which may be why they got a second chance.

grounding: Shows students whose project crashed laughing at the absurdity and then getting to work, humour giving distance without denying the hurt.

passage: The agriculture college near Dharwad had given Sarika and Darshan's group a small trial plot for their final project: three months of carefully measured millet. On Tuesday morning they arrived to find a neighbour's goats had got through the fence and eaten the whole plot. One goat was still standing in the middle, chewing. The group stared. Then Darshan said, very seriously, "Well, the goats rate our millet ten out of ten." Sarika burst out laughing. Soon they all were, clutching each other in the mud. The goat looked at them and kept chewing. When the laughter faded, Sarika said, "Okay. It hurts. Three months." "It does." They sat on the fence and planned: repair it, replant a smaller section, and use the goat damage as a case study on crop protection. Their professor loved the idea.

passage:
Diary, Friday night. Aditi.

Group dinner tonight. Zeenat was hilarious as always, doing impressions of her boss, the waiter, everyone. The whole table was crying with laughter.

Then Ravi asked her, "How's your dad doing? Is he out of hospital?" And she said, "Oh, he's fine, he's just enjoying the room service," and did a nurse impression. Everyone laughed again. And the topic was gone.

I've noticed this for months. Every time someone asks her something real, she makes a joke. She never answers.

After dinner, when everyone was getting auto-rickshaws, I walked with her to the bus stop. She'd gone quiet. I said, "You don't have to be funny with me. How's your dad really?" She didn't say anything for a minute. Then she cried, right there at the bus stop. He's been in hospital for three weeks. She's scared. I held her hand till the bus came.

qa.q: How long has Zeenat's dad been in hospital?
qa.a: Three weeks.

qa.q: Why did Aditi wait until the walk to the bus stop to ask?
qa.a: Aditi felt concerned but sensed Zeenat wouldn't answer in front of the group, so a quiet private moment felt safer.

qa.q: What could Aditi do next to support Zeenat?
qa.a: Aditi could check in again in a few days, offer to visit the hospital with her, or just be someone she doesn't have to be funny with.

qa.q: How might Zeenat feel when Aditi says she doesn't have to be funny?
qa.a: Zeenat probably feels relieved and seen, finally able to drop the jokes and show how scared she is.

grounding: Shows a friend noticing that the funniest person in the group always deflects serious questions with a quip, and checking in privately when the joking stops.

passage: In the waiting area of the bank branch in Indore, Vaibhav and Swati sat with a token number for their home-loan appointment. Vaibhav turned to her. passage:
Diary, Friday. Zubin.

Last Monday I wrote here that Parveen is the best friend in the entire world. She shared her headphones on the bus, she laughed at all my jokes, she's basically perfect.

Well, update. Today she sat with Rehan and Mishal at lunch and didn't save my seat. Didn't even wave. So I'm done. She's a traitor. She was probably always fake. I bet she only pretended to like my jokes.

I texted her one word: "Wow." She texted back, "?? what happened??"

Whatever.

Actually, when I read my Monday entry, it's weird. It's the same person. She can't be perfect on Monday and a total traitor on Friday.

Can she?

qa.a: Rehan and Mishal.

qa.a: Zubin felt hurt and disappointed about the seat, and that strong feeling made it hard to remember Parveen's good sides at the same time.

qa.q: What could Zubin try before deciding Parveen is a traitor?
qa.a: Zubin could ask Parveen about lunch, since she seems confused, and remember both the headphones and the missed seat.

qa.q: How might Parveen feel receiving the one-word text?
qa.a: Parveen probably feels confused and worried, not knowing what she did wrong.
